# Diagnosing and Reducing Body Sway on a 2010 Acura TSX

Body sway, often described as that disorienting head-bobbing sensation during high-speed cornering, is fundamentally a suspension geometry issue rather than a software bug. On your stock 2010 Acura TSX, this behavior indicates that the chassis is twisting excessively under load because the anti-roll bars aren't effectively resisting rotational force. Your experience with the 96 Integra is instructive; those cars were built on a lower, stiffer platform where aftermarket strut bars made a perceptible difference by creating a rigid triangulation between the top and bottom of the suspension tower.

On the TSX, however, you cannot simply bolt on a bar and expect identical results due to differences in mounting points and vehicle dynamics. The most direct upgrade path is replacing or reinforcing the anti-roll bar (sway bar) links. Factory rubber bushings are designed for comfort, allowing slight flex that translates into body roll. Replacing these with polyurethane or solid bushings reduces deflection under G-force, keeping the strut mount more stable relative to the chassis. This doesn't eliminate sway but stiffens the suspension's response, making the car feel less "whippy."

If you are considering a full strut bar installation on the TSX, proceed with caution. Unlike the Integra, the TSX lacks specific factory mounting points for an aftermarket cross-member that maintains proper alignment without modification. Installing one requires fabricating brackets or drilling into the chassis rail, which voids warranties and risks compromising structural integrity if done incorrectly. The geometry of a strut bar relies on equal load distribution; if the mounting points aren't perfectly symmetrical, you can induce negative camber changes that degrade tire life and handling balance.

Another critical component is the stabilizer link bushings, located where the sway bar connects to the control arms. Over time, these rubber isolators harden or crack, losing their ability to transfer force efficiently. Replacing them with upgraded polyurethane units is a low-risk intervention that often yields immediate improvement in high-speed stability without altering the vehicle's alignment settings significantly.

Tire selection also plays a massive role in perceived sway. Stock tires on a 2010 TSX are likely run-flat variants, which have stiffer sidewalls to support the car at zero pressure but offer less grip and more wall flex under cornering loads compared to performance-oriented touring tires. Switching to a set of all-season performance tires with a lower aspect ratio can reduce body roll by increasing lateral stiffness at the contact patch.

Finally, consider whether your alignment settings are optimized for sport driving. While factory specs prioritize comfort, adjusting camber and toe within safe limits can sharpen turn-in response. However, remember that reducing sway increases understeer or oversteer characteristics; if you stiffen the rear suspension too much without tuning the front, you may compromise stability in emergency maneuvers. The goal is balance, not maximum rigidity in one direction.
